back: Low dose paroxetine, venlafaxine, escitalopram, gabapentin (nocturnal symptoms), and fezolinetant, a neurokinin 3 antagonist that needs liver enzyme monitoring. Cognitive behavioral therapy and hypnosis also work.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Hot flush treatment in a woman taking tamoxifen
back: Avoid paroxetine and fluoxetine, which inhibit the enzyme that activates tamoxifen. Choose venlafaxine or gabapentin instead.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Contraceptive typical use failure rates by tier
back: Implant, IUDs, and sterilization: under 1 per 100. Injectable: about 4. Pill, patch, ring: about 7. Male condom: about 13. Fertility awareness and withdrawal are less effective.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Category 4 conditions for combined hormonal contraception
back: Migraine with aura, current or past venous thromboembolism in most cases, thrombogenic mutations, ischemic heart disease or stroke, blood pressure 160/100 or higher, breast cancer, severe cirrhosis, and lupus with positive antiphospholipid antibodies.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Combined hormonal contraception in the postpartum period
back: Category 4 in the first 21 days postpartum because of thrombotic risk. Use progestin only methods or the copper IUD, which are safe alternatives when estrogen is the concern.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Main drawbacks of medroxyprogesterone acetate and the copper IUD
back: Medroxyprogesterone lowers bone density during use, which recovers after stopping, and may cause weight gain. The copper IUD is hormone free but can increase menstrual bleeding and cramping.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Most effective emergency contraception
back: The copper IUD, failure near 0.1 percent, placed within five days. Ulipristal 30 mg works up to 120 hours and beats levonorgestrel 1.5 mg, which is best within 72 hours, especially in obesity.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Starting a hormonal method after ulipristal
back: Wait five days before starting a hormonal method and use a barrier method until then, because ulipristal binds the progesterone receptor and the hormone could blunt its effect.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Federal consent rules for publicly funded sterilization
back: Age at least 21, with consent signed at least 30 days and no more than 180 days before the procedure. Counsel on regret and permanence.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Salpingectomy versus tubal occlusion for sterilization
back: Bilateral salpingectomy is preferred where feasible because removing the tubes lowers ovarian cancer risk. A failed tubal sterilization carries an increased proportion of ectopic pregnancies.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Vasectomy follow up
back: Safer, cheaper, and as effective as tubal sterilization, but a semen analysis must confirm azoospermia before unprotected intercourse. Neither procedure protects against infection.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Lactational amenorrhea method criteria
back: Effective only when the infant is under six months, exclusively breastfed, and the mother is amenorrheic. Lactating women can also use progestin only methods and copper IUDs.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: FIGO classification of abnormal uterine bleeding
back: PALM COEIN. Structural: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy or hyperplasia. Nonstructural: coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not yet classified.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Indications for endometrial sampling in abnormal bleeding
back: Age 45 or older, younger patients with unopposed estrogen exposure such as obesity or chronic anovulation, persistent bleeding, or failed medical therapy. A normal ultrasound does not replace the biopsy.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: First line treatment of heavy bleeding without a structural lesion
back: The levonorgestrel IUD. Alternatives: combined hormonal contraception, oral progestins, and tranexamic acid during menses, which is avoided with thromboembolic risk. NSAIDs reduce loss modestly.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Heavy bleeding in an adolescent
back: Often anovulation, but a substantial minority have a bleeding disorder, most often von Willebrand disease. Draw von Willebrand studies before estrogen, which raises factor levels and masks the disorder.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Acute heavy uterine bleeding: stable versus unstable
back: Stable: multi dose combined oral contraceptive or high dose progestin. Unstable: resuscitation and intravenous conjugated estrogen, sometimes curettage or intrauterine balloon tamponade.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Fibroid versus adenomyosis on examination and imaging
back: Fibroid is a discrete firm rounded mass with a pseudocapsule. Adenomyosis is a diffusely enlarged, tender, boggy uterus without a clear border, with heavy menses and dysmenorrhea in a parous woman. Myomectomy is not an option for it.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Medical therapy for symptomatic fibroids
back: Levonorgestrel IUD if the cavity is undistorted, combined contraception, tranexamic acid, and NSAIDs reduce bleeding. GnRH antagonists with add back reduce bleeding and volume. Agonists are a temporary bridge before surgery.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Uterine artery embolization for fibroids
back: Minimally invasive option for a woman who wants to keep her uterus and does not desire pregnancy. Fertility outcome is less certain than after myomectomy, and symptoms can recur.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Myomectomy and later labor
back: Preferred for fibroids in a woman who wants to conceive. Deep intramural myomectomy entering the cavity raises uterine rupture risk in labor, so plan cesarean birth before labor.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Endometrial polyp: when to remove
back: Hysteroscopic polypectomy with histology for symptomatic polyps, any polyp with postmenopausal bleeding, or in infertility. Tamoxifen raises polyp risk. Small asymptomatic premenopausal polyps may be observed.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Pelvic pain syndromes: key clues
back: Vulvodynia: cotton swab vestibular pain. Bladder pain syndrome: pain relieved by voiding, sterile urine. Pelvic congestion: dull pain worse on standing. Ovarian remnant: cyclic pain after oophorectomy.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Ultrasound criteria diagnostic of early pregnancy failure
back: Crown rump length 7 mm or more with no cardiac activity, or mean sac diameter 25 mm or more with no embryo. Sac 16 to 24 mm without an embryo is suspicious, so repeat the scan in 7 to 10 days.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Medical management of early pregnancy loss
back: Mifepristone 200 mg orally then misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally is most effective; misoprostol alone is acceptable. Aspiration is preferred for heavy bleeding, instability, or infection.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Minimum expected 48 hour hCG rise in early pregnancy
back: About 49 percent below 1,500 mIU/mL, 40 percent from 1,500 to 3,000, and 33 percent above 3,000. A slower rise is suspicious but does not locate the pregnancy.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Discriminatory hCG level
back: The value above which an intrauterine sac should be seen. If used, set conservatively high, up to 3,500 mIU/mL. Never use it alone to end a pregnancy that may be desired.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Single dose methotrexate regimen for ectopic pregnancy
back: 50 mg per square meter on day 1, check hCG on days 4 and 7. A fall of at least 15 percent allows weekly monitoring; a smaller fall needs a second dose or surgery. Avoid folate and NSAIDs.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Contraindications to methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy
back: Intrauterine pregnancy, breastfeeding, immunodeficiency, significant liver or kidney disease, blood dyscrasia, active pulmonary disease, peptic ulcer disease, hypersensitivity, and rupture or instability.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Adnexal torsion: diagnosis and management
back: Sudden severe unilateral pain with nausea and an adnexal mass. Normal Doppler flow does not exclude it. Laparoscopic detorsion with ovarian preservation, even when the ovary looks dark.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Mature cystic teratoma
back: Most common benign ovarian neoplasm in reproductive age women, with an echogenic nodule and shadowing. It is the neoplasm most prone to torsion. Treat symptomatic or growing lesions with ovarian cystectomy.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Outpatient treatment of pelvic inflammatory disease
back: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days, and metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 14 days. Treat empirically without waiting for test results, and treat partners.
area: Reproductive endocrinology, contraception, and benign gynecology

front: Cervical screening for women under 21
back: No screening, even with early sexual activity. Screening begins at 21 under the USPSTF and at 25 under the American Cancer Society.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Screening options for ages 21 to 29 and the role of HPV testing
back: Cytology alone every 3 years. HPV testing is not used alone in this age group.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Screening options for ages 30 to 65
back: Cytology every 3 years, high risk HPV testing alone every 5 years, or cotesting every 5 years. The American Cancer Society prefers primary HPV testing every 5 years.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Criteria to stop cervical screening at 65
back: Adequate negative screening: 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 negative cotests within 10 years, most recent within 5 years, and no CIN 2 or higher in the past 25 years.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Chemoprevention for breast cancer: tamoxifen versus raloxifene
back: Tamoxifen works pre and postmenopause but raises thromboembolism, endometrial cancer, and cataracts. Raloxifene is postmenopausal only without endometrial risk. Neither is used with prior thromboembolism.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: BI-RADS categories 0 through 6 and actions
back: 0 incomplete, more imaging. 1 or 2 negative or benign, routine. 3 probably benign, short interval follow up. 4 suspicious, biopsy. 5 highly suggestive, biopsy and referral. 6 known cancer.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Immediate CIN 3 plus risk threshold that triggers colposcopy
back: An immediate risk of 4 percent or more reaches the colposcopy threshold under the 2019 risk based consensus guidelines. Surveillance intervals rest on the 5 year risk.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Physiologic versus pathologic nipple discharge
back: Physiologic: bilateral, multiductal, on compression, check pregnancy, prolactin, thyroid, drugs. Pathologic: spontaneous, unilateral, single duct, clear or bloody, usually intraductal papilloma; image and excise the duct.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Management of atypical glandular cells on cytology
back: Colposcopy with endocervical sampling, plus endometrial sampling from age 35, or earlier with obesity, abnormal bleeding, or Lynch syndrome.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Treatment of CIN 2 or CIN 3 in a nonpregnant woman
back: Excision by loop electrosurgical procedure or cold knife conization, which gives a margin specimen. Ablation needs a fully visible transformation zone and no glandular disease.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Management of CIN 2 or CIN 3 in pregnancy
back: Observe, do not treat, unless invasion is suspected. Biopsy is safe, endocervical curettage is not performed, and conization is reserved for suspected invasive cancer.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Management of adenocarcinoma in situ of the cervix
back: Diagnostic excision with clean margins, then hysterectomy once childbearing is complete. It can skip lesions in the canal, so ablation and simple observation are inadequate.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: FIGO 2018 cervical stage IA1 versus IA2
back: IA1 has stromal invasion of 3 mm or less. IA2 has invasion over 3 mm but under 5 mm. IA1 without vascular invasion is treated by conization, which preserves fertility.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Cervical cancer stage IB subdivisions by tumor size
back: IB1 under 2 cm, IB2 from 2 to under 4 cm, IB3 4 cm or more. Stages IB1 to IIA1 get radical hysterectomy with node assessment.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Treatment of cervical cancer stage IB3 through IVA
back: Cisplatin based chemoradiation. Surgery is not first line. Pelvic node involvement upstages to IIIC1 and para aortic nodes to IIIC2.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Usual type versus differentiated type vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia
back: Usual type: HPV related, younger women, often multifocal. Differentiated type: HPV unrelated, older women, arises in lichen sclerosus, often TP53 mutated, single lesion, progresses quickly to cancer.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: First step for a raised, pigmented, ulcerated, or persistent white or red vulvar lesion
back: Biopsy. Empiric treatment for weeks without tissue is the error that delays the diagnosis of vulvar carcinoma.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Lichen sclerosus: findings and first line treatment
back: Itching, thin white parchment skin, labial loss, clitoral burying, and figure eight fissures. Treat with clobetasol 0.05 percent ointment, tapered to maintenance, with lifelong follow up for carcinoma.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva
back: Red eczematous plaque that fails steroids or antifungals. Biopsy shows pale Paget cells. Evaluate for underlying adenocarcinoma and distant cancers. Treat with wide local excision; recurrence is common.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Evaluation of a new Bartholin gland mass in a woman over 40
back: Biopsy or excise it instead of repeated drainage, because drainage will not treat a carcinoma.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Vulvar cancer: first nodal drainage and sentinel node role
back: Spreads first to inguinofemoral nodes. Unifocal tumors under 4 cm get sentinel node biopsy, which reduces lymphedema. Stage IA (2 cm or less, 1 mm invasion or less) needs only wide local excision.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Clinical picture of in utero diethylstilbestrol exposure
back: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of vagina and cervix, vaginal adenosis, T shaped uterus, cervical collar and hood, plus preterm birth and ectopic pregnancy risk.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Postmenopausal bleeding: initial evaluation and thin stripe threshold
back: Transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial biopsy. A stripe of 4 mm or less allows observation if bleeding does not recur. Thicker stripe or persistent bleeding needs tissue.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Triple assessment of a palpable breast mass
back: Clinical examination, imaging, and tissue sampling. Under 30: ultrasound first. Age 30 or older: diagnostic mammogram plus ultrasound. Core needle biopsy is preferred over fine needle aspiration.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Management of endometrial hyperplasia without atypia
back: Progestin, either continuous oral therapy or the levonorgestrel intrauterine device, then repeat biopsy to confirm regression. Add weight loss when obesity drives the process.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Atypical endometrial hyperplasia: treatment and fertility sparing option
back: Hysterectomy after childbearing, since many have coexisting carcinoma. Fertility sparing: high dose progestin with biopsy every 3 to 6 months, then hysterectomy if disease persists.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Lynch syndrome genes and endometrial tumor screening step
back: MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, and EPCAM deletion. Test tumors for mismatch repair loss. If MLH1 is absent, test promoter methylation: methylation means sporadic tumor, not germline.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Lynch syndrome carrier gynecologic management
back: Consider annual endometrial biopsy from age 30 to 35, and risk reducing hysterectomy with salpingo oophorectomy after childbearing. Colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years from age 20 to 25.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Aggressive endometrial histologies and the four molecular groups
back: Serous, clear cell, and carcinosarcoma are aggressive. Molecular groups: POLE mutated (best prognosis), mismatch repair deficient, no specific profile, p53 abnormal (worst).
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Why power morcellation is avoided when malignancy is possible
back: It can disseminate an unsuspected leiomyosarcoma. No reliable preoperative test exists, so suspect rapid growth in a postmenopausal woman or a necrotic heterogeneous mass.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Tamoxifen effect on the uterus and screening of asymptomatic users
back: Estrogen agonist in the uterus, raising endometrial cancer risk. Asymptomatic women are not screened with ultrasound or biopsy; any bleeding is evaluated.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Ovarian cancer screening in average risk women
back: No test lowers mortality. Transvaginal ultrasound with CA-125 is not recommended. Opportunistic salpingectomy at hysterectomy reflects the fimbrial origin of high grade serous cancer.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Risk reducing salpingo oophorectomy timing for BRCA1 versus BRCA2
back: BRCA1 carriers at 35 to 40 years, BRCA2 carriers at 40 to 45 years, after childbearing. It also lowers breast cancer risk if done before menopause.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Who gets genetic testing among ovarian cancer patients
back: Every woman with epithelial ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer regardless of family history. Other risk genes include RAD51C, RAD51D, BRIP1, and Lynch genes.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Why cyst aspiration or biopsy is avoided for a suspicious adnexal mass
back: Spill upstages a cancer. Refer to a gynecologic oncologist for surgery. CA-125 is raised in many benign states, so it is most useful postmenopause and for monitoring.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Ovarian tumor markers: dysgerminoma, yolk sac, embryonal carcinoma
back: Dysgerminoma: LDH. Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumor: alpha fetoprotein. Embryonal carcinoma: alpha fetoprotein plus hCG. Markers aid monitoring but never replace pathology.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: First line chemotherapy for epithelial ovarian cancer and maintenance therapy
back: Carboplatin with paclitaxel, neoadjuvant if upfront resection is unsafe. PARP inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib) maintain response, best with BRCA or homologous recombination deficiency; anemia and rare MDS or AML.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: hCG surveillance after molar evacuation
back: Baseline within 48 hours, then weekly until undetectable on 3 consecutive weekly samples, then monthly. Use reliable contraception; place an intrauterine device only after hCG is undetectable.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia: low risk versus high risk treatment
back: FIGO score 6 or less is low risk: single agent methotrexate or dactinomycin. Score 7 or more is high risk: multiagent chemotherapy. Placental site and epithelioid tumors: hysterectomy.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Chemotherapy timing for cancer in pregnancy
back: Avoid in the first trimester. Second and third trimesters are acceptable, stopping about 3 weeks before delivery. Avoid pelvic radiation and gadolinium; necessary imaging is not withheld.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Stress versus urgency incontinence: mechanism and first line therapy
back: Stress: weak urethral closure with cough or lifting, pelvic floor training. Urgency: detrusor overactivity with sudden need to void, bladder training. Mixed: treat predominant symptom first.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Antimuscarinic drugs for overactive bladder: examples, effects, cautions
back: Oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin, fesoterodine, trospium. Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision. Avoid in narrow angle glaucoma and gastric retention; mirabegron is the alternative but can raise blood pressure.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Midurethral sling: routes and complications
back: Retropubic has higher bladder perforation risk; transobturator has more groin pain. Others: voiding dysfunction, mesh exposure, de novo urgency. Delay sling surgery if future pregnancies are planned.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: POP-Q examination: points measured and how stage is assigned
back: Aa, Ba, Ap, Bp, C, D plus genital hiatus, perineal body, and total vaginal length, relative to the hymen. Stage is set by the most distal prolapse; a large hiatus predicts recurrence.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: First line management of symptomatic prolapse
back: Pessary at any stage, with vaginal estrogen to lower erosion risk, and pelvic floor training. Asymptomatic prolapse needs no treatment. A pessary may unmask stress incontinence.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Apical prolapse repairs: uterosacral versus sacrospinous fixation, and sacrocolpopexy
back: Uterosacral: ureteral kinking, so cystoscopy after repair. Sacrospinous: buttock pain. Sacrocolpopexy with mesh is most durable; Burch at sacrocolpopexy lowers later stress incontinence. Colpocleisis suits older women not sexually active.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Obstetric laceration grades: third degree subdivisions and fourth degree
back: 3a: under half of external sphincter torn. 3b: more than half. 3c: internal sphincter also torn. Fourth degree: both sphincters plus anal epithelium. Always perform a rectal examination.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Obstetric anal sphincter repair technique and perioperative care
back: Close rectal mucosa first, repair internal sphincter separately, then external sphincter end to end or overlapping with delayed absorbable suture. Give one dose of a second generation cephalosporin and stool softeners; avoid opioids.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Vesicovaginal versus ureterovaginal fistula dye test
back: Methylene blue in the bladder stains a vaginal tampon blue for a vesicovaginal fistula. A wet but unstained tampon suggests a ureterovaginal fistula. Cause is usually bladder injury at hysterectomy.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Rectovaginal fistula: causes and repair timing
back: Obstetric injury (missed fourth degree tear or breakdown), Crohn disease, radiation, malignancy. Delay repair until inflammation and infection settle; complex tracts may need temporary diversion.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Definition and prevention of recurrent urinary tract infection
back: Two in 6 months or three in 1 year, each culture confirmed. Vaginal estrogen after menopause, methenamine hippurate, or antibiotic prophylaxis for 6 to 12 months or postcoital.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a nonpregnant woman
back: Do not screen or treat, except before urologic procedures that breach the mucosa.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Microscopic hematuria definition and work up
back: Three or more RBC per high power field on one properly collected specimen. Treat any infection and retest, then risk stratify: cystoscopy plus renal ultrasound (intermediate) or cross sectional imaging (high). Anticoagulants do not explain it.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome) treatment steps
back: Clinical diagnosis after excluding infection, stones, endometriosis, and cancer. First line: education, triggers, pelvic floor therapy. Then amitriptyline, hydroxyzine, pentosan polysulfate (maculopathy warning), instillations; fulgurate Hunner lesions.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Urethral diverticulum triad and best imaging; ureteral injury sites
back: Dysuria, dyspareunia, postvoid dribbling; MRI is best. Ureter is at risk under the uterine artery, at the pelvic brim near the infundibulopelvic ligament, and along the cardinal ligament.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Bacterial vaginosis: Amsel criteria and treatment
back: Three of four: thin homogeneous discharge, pH above 4.5, clue cells, positive whiff test. Treat with oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days, metronidazole gel, or clindamycin cream.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Vulvovaginal candidiasis: findings and complicated disease treatment
back: Normal pH, budding yeast and pseudohyphae. Uncomplicated: topical azole or fluconazole 150 mg once. Complicated or recurrent: 7 to 14 days, then weekly fluconazole for 6 months; C. glabrata may need boric acid.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Trichomoniasis diagnosis and treatment
back: Frothy yellow green discharge, pH above 4.5, strawberry cervix. NAAT is more sensitive than wet mount. Metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days, treat partners, retest in 3 months.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Atrophic vaginitis versus desquamative inflammatory vaginitis
back: Atrophic: raised pH, parabasal cells, treat with vaginal estrogen, prasterone, or ospemifene. Desquamative: purulent discharge, parabasal cells, many leukocytes, lost lactobacilli, treat with clindamycin cream.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Erosive lichen planus of the vulva and vagina
back: Painful erosions, white lacy border, scarring, and vaginal synechiae. Unlike lichen sclerosus it involves the vagina. Biopsy confirms; treat with high potency topical steroids, including vaginal steroid suppositories.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Drugs for hypoactive sexual desire in premenopausal women
back: Flibanserin (daily, risk of hypotension and syncope) and bremelanotide (on demand injection). Check for serotonin reuptake inhibitor effects; bupropion may correct them. Testosterone is not approved for women in the United States.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Provoked vestibulodynia: diagnosis and treatment
back: Cotton swab touch at the 4 and 8 o'clock vestibule reproduces pain. Treat with pelvic floor physical therapy, dilators, topical lidocaine, and sometimes a low dose tricyclic.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Prepubertal vulvovaginitis: causes and management
back: Usually nonspecific from hypoestrogenic mucosa and hygiene: sitz baths, cotton clothing, barrier ointment. Group A strep gives sharp erythema, Shigella bloody discharge, pinworm nocturnal itching (tape test).
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Persistent bloody or foul vaginal discharge in a prepubertal girl
back: Suspect a foreign body, usually toilet paper: saline irrigation, or vaginoscopy under anesthesia. Button batteries and magnets are urgent. Grape like mass is sarcoma botryoides, needing biopsy.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Labial adhesions in girls: treatment
back: Observe if asymptomatic. Topical estrogen cream for several weeks if obstruction or infection occurs, then an emollient. Avoid forceful manual separation, which is painful and relapses.
area: Gynecologic oncology, breast, urogynecology, and lower tract

front: Pelvic examination at the well woman visit for an asymptomatic patient
back: A shared decision, not required at every visit. It is not needed to prescribe contraception or to collect a cervical screening sample.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Tdap and RSV vaccine timing in pregnancy
back: Tdap once in every pregnancy, preferably early in the 27 to 36 week window, even if given last year. RSV vaccine is offered at 32 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks in season.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Live vaccines and pregnancy
back: Measles, mumps, rubella and varicella vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy. Give them postpartum to women without immunity. Influenza vaccine is given yearly, and recombinant zoster is a two dose series from age 50.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Lung cancer screening criteria
back: Annual low dose CT for ages 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack years who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Diabetes screening and statin criteria in adults
back: Screen glucose at ages 35 to 70 with overweight or obesity, earlier after gestational diabetes. Statin at ages 40 to 75 with one risk factor and 10 year risk of 10 percent or more.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Who is screened for chlamydia and gonorrhea
back: All sexually active women aged 24 or younger, and older women with a new partner, multiple partners, or an infected partner. Nucleic acid amplification on a vaginal swab, which may be self collected.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Treatment of uncomplicated chlamydia, nonpregnant and pregnant
back: Nonpregnant: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. Pregnant: azithromycin 1 g once, because doxycycline is avoided. Test of cure about 4 weeks after treatment in pregnancy.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Treatment of uncomplicated gonorrhea
back: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once (1 g if 150 kg or more). Add doxycycline if chlamydia is not excluded. Routine second gonorrhea drug is no longer used. Retest at 3 months.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Partner management for chlamydia and gonorrhea
back: Evaluate partners with contact in the previous 60 days. Expedited partner therapy gives medication or a prescription without a visit and suits heterosexual partners. Report the infection to the health department.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Syphilis stages and the findings of each
back: Primary: painless indurated chancre. Secondary: diffuse rash including palms and soles, mucous patches, condylomata lata. Latent: positive serology only. Tertiary: gummatous, cardiovascular, neurologic. Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Syphilis treatment and follow up
back: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once for primary, secondary, or early latent disease; weekly for 3 doses for late latent or unknown duration. Pregnant with allergy: desensitize. Titers should fall fourfold.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Jarisch Herxheimer reaction
back: Transient fever, myalgia, and headache within 24 hours of starting treatment for syphilis. It is not penicillin allergy. Treat symptomatically and continue therapy.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Genital herpes diagnosis and treatment
back: Diagnose by NAAT or culture of lesion fluid, not routine serology. First episode: valacyclovir or acyclovir for 7 to 10 days. Frequent recurrences: daily suppression, which lowers but does not remove transmission.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: HIV preexposure prophylaxis options for women
back: Daily oral emtricitabine with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, injectable cabotegravir every 2 months, or lenacapavir every 6 months. Tenofovir alafenamide is not preferred for receptive vaginal sex. Retest about every 3 months.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Hypertension categories and when to start drugs
back: Elevated 120 to 129 over under 80; stage 1 is 130 to 139 or 80 to 89; stage 2 is 140 over 90 or higher. Treat stage 1 with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, kidney disease, or risk 7.5 percent or more.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Atypical presentations of myocardial infarction in women
back: Fatigue, dyspnea, nausea, and jaw, neck, or back pain more often than crushing chest pressure. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection and stress cardiomyopathy are more common in women and can follow childbirth.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Diagnostic thresholds for diabetes and prediabetes
back: Diabetes: A1c 6.5 percent or more, fasting glucose 126 or more, 2 hour 75 g load 200 or more, or random 200 or more with symptoms. Prediabetes: A1c 5.7 to 6.4 or fasting 100 to 125.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Hypothyroidism and iron deficiency anemia diagnosis and treatment
back: Hypothyroidism: high TSH with low free T4, levothyroxine, recheck TSH in 6 to 8 weeks. Iron deficiency: low ferritin with low MCV, oral iron daily or alternate days, intravenous if intolerant.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Migraine with aura and hormonal contraception
back: Migraine with aura raises stroke risk, so avoid estrogen containing contraception. Sudden severe headache, neurologic deficit, or new headache after age 50 needs imaging.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Osteoporosis diagnosis and first line therapy
back: T score of minus 2.5 or lower, or a fragility hip or spine fracture. Oral bisphosphonates first, zoledronic acid yearly if pills fail. Stopping denosumab without a follow on agent causes rebound vertebral fractures.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: FRAX treatment thresholds in osteopenia
back: Treat when 10 year risk is 20 percent or more for major osteoporotic fracture or 3 percent or more for hip fracture. Reassess long term bisphosphonate use after several years.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Screening tools for depression and anxiety
back: PHQ 2 and PHQ 9 for depression, GAD 7 for anxiety. A score of 10 or more suggests moderate symptoms. Ask every positive screen directly about suicidal thoughts.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Before starting an antidepressant, ask about what
back: Past mania or hypomania, because an antidepressant alone can provoke mania in bipolar disorder. An SSRI such as sertraline or escitalopram is the usual first drug.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Diagnosis of premenstrual dysphoric disorder
back: At least five symptoms in the week before menses, one affective, improving within days of bleeding and minimal the week after. Confirm with two cycles of daily ratings. Symptoms present all month suggest a mood disorder.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating compared
back: Anorexia: restriction, bradycardia, lanugo, hypothermia. Bulimia: purging, parotid enlargement, dental erosion, hypokalemia, alkalosis; fluoxetine helps, avoid bupropion. Binge eating: binges without compensation, linked to obesity.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Tobacco cessation approach
back: Five steps: ask, advise, assess readiness, assist, arrange follow up. Varenicline is the most effective single drug; combination nicotine replacement is nearly as good. Combine drug therapy with counseling.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Opioid, stimulant, and cannabis use disorder treatment
back: Opioids: buprenorphine or methadone, continued and not tapered quickly, plus naloxone. Stimulants and cannabis: no approved drug, so use behavioral therapy and contingency management.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Intimate partner violence screening rules
back: Screen reproductive age women, including pregnant and postpartum, with a validated tool. Ask in private with a professional interpreter if needed. Positive screen: validate, assess safety, plan, refer. Learn state reporting rules.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Presumptive STI treatment after sexual assault
back: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days, and metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days. Give hepatitis B and HPV vaccines if not complete.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: HIV prophylaxis and emergency contraception after sexual assault
back: Start HIV prophylaxis within 72 hours of substantial exposure for 28 days. Offer emergency contraception up to 120 hours: copper IUD most effective, then ulipristal, then levonorgestrel.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Adolescent confidentiality and its limits
back: Interview alone for part of every visit. Limits are serious harm to the patient or others and mandatory abuse reports. Most states let minors consent to contraception, STI care, and pregnancy care. First gynecologic visit at 13 to 15.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: HPV vaccine schedule
back: Routine at 11 to 12, may start at 9. Under 15: two doses at least 5 months apart. Age 15 or older, or immunocompromised: three doses at 0, 1 to 2, and 6 months. Catch up through 26; shared decision 27 to 45.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Normal adolescent cycle and when to evaluate
back: Cycle length 21 to 45 days with bleeding up to 7 days. Persistent cycles outside the range, or longer than 90 days, need evaluation. Menses is treated as a vital sign.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Primary dysmenorrhea management
back: Prostaglandin mediated pain starting within a year or two of menarche. NSAID at onset of bleeding first, hormonal contraception second. Failure after about 3 months suggests endometriosis.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Transgender hormone therapy and contraception counseling
back: Transgender women: estradiol plus spironolactone, thrombosis risk highest with oral estrogen. Transgender men: testosterone stops menses but is not contraception, and hematocrit is monitored for erythrocytosis.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Red flags for hereditary breast and ovarian cancer
back: Young onset or triple negative or bilateral or male breast cancer, ovarian, tubal, or peritoneal cancer at any age, pancreatic cancer, multiple related cancers, and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. Refer for genetic counseling.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: BRCA carrier inheritance, imaging, and testing counseling
back: Autosomal dominant, 50 percent chance for each child. Annual breast MRI plus mammography when lifetime risk is 20 percent or more. A variant of uncertain significance does not change management.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Limits of the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act
back: Protects against discrimination in health insurance and employment. It does not cover life, disability, or long term care insurance. Tell patients before testing.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Lynch syndrome recognition and office follow up
back: Mismatch repair gene variant or EPCAM deletion. Suspect with young colorectal or endometrial cancer or clustered related cancers. Earlier, more frequent colonoscopy, prompt endometrial sampling for abnormal bleeding, and cascade testing of relatives.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Geriatric gynecology cervical screening and medication review
back: Stop cervical screening at 65 after adequate negative results, but continue breast care and sexual history. Review anticholinergics and sedatives, which worsen cognition and increase falls.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Hysterectomy route hierarchy for benign disease
back: Vaginal is preferred, then laparoscopic or robotic, then abdominal. Choose open surgery only for a very large uterus, extensive disease, suspected malignancy needing intact removal, or limited access.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Laparoscopic entry injuries
back: Greatest danger at first trocar placement. Aorta and iliac vessels lie below the umbilicus. Open and closed entry have similar complication rates. Expanding retroperitoneal hematoma or hypotension after insufflation needs laparotomy.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Course of the ureter and sites of injury
back: Crosses the pelvic brim at the common iliac bifurcation, passes beneath the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix. Injury clusters at the infundibulopelvic ligament, uterine artery pedicle, and cardinal and uterosacral ligaments.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Preoperative cardiac risk assessment
back: Weigh urgency of surgery, then functional capacity (4 METs, two flights of stairs, usually proceeds). Revised Cardiac Risk Index: high risk surgery, ischemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin, creatinine above 2.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Perioperative medicine management
back: Continue beta blockers and statins; do not start a beta blocker on the day of surgery. Stop SGLT2 inhibitors 3 to 4 days before. Hold warfarin about 5 days. Continue aspirin with a coronary stent.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Procedures that do not need antibiotic prophylaxis
back: Diagnostic laparoscopy, hysteroscopy, dilation and curettage, hysterosalpingography without dilated tubes, and IUD insertion. Hysterectomy by any route does need it.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Cefazolin prophylaxis details
back: Within 60 minutes before incision; 2 g, or 3 g at 120 kg or more. Redose after 4 hours or blood loss over 1,500 mL. True immediate penicillin reaction: clindamycin or vancomycin with an aminoglycoside or aztreonam.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis by risk category
back: Low: ambulation. Moderate: compression devices or drug. High: compression plus drug. Cancer surgery: extend drug up to 4 weeks. Drug unsafe because of bleeding: compression devices only.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Local anesthetic ceilings and toxicity
back: Lidocaine 4.5 mg/kg, or 7 mg/kg with epinephrine. Toxicity: perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, then seizures and arrest. Stop injection, support airway, treat seizures, give lipid emulsion.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Positioning nerve injuries and deficits
back: Common peroneal: foot drop from leg holder. Femoral: weak knee extension from retractor or hip flexion. Obturator: weak adduction. Lateral femoral cutaneous: numbness without weakness. Brachial plexus: arm abducted past 90 degrees.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Electrosurgical injury mechanisms in laparoscopy
back: Insulation failure, direct coupling to another metal instrument, and capacitive coupling through intact insulation. Bowel burns present 3 to 7 days later with fever, pain, and peritonitis. Bipolar is safer near ureter and bowel.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Well leg compartment syndrome
back: Prolonged lithotomy then reperfusion causes calf swelling. Pain out of proportion, pain on passive toe stretch, tense calf, normal pulses possible. Measure pressures, fasciotomy, fluids for myoglobin.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Distending media pairing with energy and the complication of each
back: Saline with bipolar or mechanical tools: volume overload, pulmonary edema. Glycine, sorbitol, mannitol with monopolar: hyponatremia, cerebral edema; glycine adds hyperammonemia. Carbon dioxide is for diagnostic use only.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Distending media fluid deficit stop thresholds
back: Stop and check electrolytes at a deficit of 1,000 mL of electrolyte free fluid or 2,500 mL of saline in a healthy woman. Treat with a loop diuretic and correct sodium slowly; hypertonic saline only for severe neurologic symptoms.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Uterine perforation during curettage or hysteroscopy
back: Blunt dilator or sound and a stable patient: observe. Energy device, resectoscope loop, or suction active: laparoscopy or laparotomy to inspect bowel, bladder, and broad ligament. Lateral perforations can form a broad ligament hematoma.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Timing and physiology of unrecognized bowel injury at laparoscopy
back: Fever, rising pain, and high white count on postoperative day 3 to 5. Pneumoperitoneum reduces venous return and absorbs carbon dioxide. Shoulder pain comes from residual gas under the diaphragm.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Sterilization failure and the ectopic pregnancy rule
back: Ten year cumulative pregnancy risk was 18.5 per 1,000, higher in younger women, with about a third ectopic. Any pregnancy after sterilization is ectopic until proved otherwise.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Endometrial ablation prerequisites
back: Completed childbearing, normal cavity, and prior biopsy to exclude hyperplasia and cancer. It is not contraception, and later cyclic pain may signal hematometra.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Postoperative fever by day
back: Hours: drug or transfusion reaction, malignant hyperthermia (dantrolene). Days 1 to 2: necrotizing infection, aspiration. Day 3: urinary infection. Days 4 to 5: clot, cuff infection, abscess. Days 5 to 7: wound infection.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Postoperative ileus versus small bowel obstruction versus Ogilvie syndrome
back: Ileus: 2 to 3 days, no flatus, supportive care. Obstruction: colicky pain, vomiting, obstipation, transition point; bowel rest and nasogastric decompression. Ogilvie: massive cecal dilation, treat with decompression and neostigmine.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Management of bladder and ureteral injury
back: Bladder dome laceration: two layer closure, backfill test, catheter 7 to 14 days. Ureter: stent for partial injury, end to end repair mid ureter, ureteroneocystostomy with psoas hitch distally. Fluid creatinine far above serum confirms urine.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Vaginal cuff evisceration management
back: Do not push the bowel back. Cover with moist saline gauze, keep fasting, give broad spectrum antibiotics, and go to the operating room for repair and visceral inspection.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Necrotizing fasciitis versus simple surgical site infection
back: Simple infection (days 5 to 7): open and drain, antibiotics if cellulitis spreads. Necrotizing: pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, instability; emergent debridement plus broad antibiotics including clindamycin.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: LEEP, cold knife cone, and colposcopy complications
back: Colposcopy: directed biopsy. LEEP: transformation zone under local anesthesia, delayed bleeding at 1 to 2 weeks, stenosis, later preterm birth. Cold knife cone for suspected invasion or glandular lesion.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care

front: Bartholin abscess treatment and cerclage technique
back: Drain with Word catheter for 4 to 6 weeks or marsupialize; antibiotics only for cellulitis. Biopsy at age 40 or older. McDonald cerclage is the usual purse string, removed at 36 to 37 weeks.
area: Office practice and peri-operative care
